passages.title: Abu Lahab and his wife doomed
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

This short sūrah is Allah's answer to one man's public insult of His Messenger ﷺ. Abu Lahab — the Prophet's ﷺ own uncle — mocked him in front of the assembled Quraysh, and Allah replied with five ayat that pronounce ruin on him, strip away the wealth and children he was counting on, name the Fire he will enter, and place his wife beside him in it. What holds the five ayat together is a single arc: a curse (ayah 1), the collapse of everything he trusted (ayah 2), his destination (ayah 3), and his partner in the crime sharing his punishment (ayat 4–5).

## The moment on the mountain

Ibn Kathir records from **al-Bukhari**, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ went out to the valley of al-Baṭḥā and ascended the mountain. Then he cried out *"Yā ṣabāḥāh!"* — rendered there as "O people, come at once!" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this call as being made "in a manner that was known among them for warning of an attack by the enemy." The Quraysh gathered around him. He ﷺ asked them: *"If I told you all that the enemy was going to attack you in the morning, or in the evening, would you all believe me?"* They replied, "Yes." Then he said: *"Verily, I am a warner (sent) to you all before the coming of a severe torment."*

They had just conceded, publicly, that his word was good. And then his uncle broke the moment. Abu Lahab said: **"Have you gathered us for this? May you perish!"** Another narration in Ibn Kathir adds a detail that makes the scene vivid — he stood up *dusting off his hands* and said, "Perish you for the rest of this day! Have you gathered us for this?"

So Allah revealed this sūrah, to the end.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the episode after the revelation of *"Warn your closest relatives"* (26:214), and reports the same event as recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, with the Prophet ﷺ ascending Mount Ṣafā — and, in some narratives, calling the Makkan clans by name, Banū ʿAbd Manāf, Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and others. In that account Abu Lahab responded *"Tabban laka!"* — "Ruin may seize you! Is it for this purpose that you have called us together?" — and picked up a stone to hit him ﷺ.

So the man's insult was itself an imprecation, a calling down of ruin on the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Maʿārif tells us what happened next: the Muslims longed for that imprecation to be turned back on him, and Allah both invoked it and informed them that it had already taken effect. We will come to that in ayah 1.

## Who Abu Lahab was

Ibn Kathir tells us he was one of the uncles of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. His name was **ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib**, his surname was **Abū ʿUtaybah**, and he was called *Abu Lahab* — "Father of Flame" — only because of the brightness of his face. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same nickname and explains it by his ruddy complexion. Ibn Kathir: "He used to often cause harm to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He hated and scorned him and his religion." Maʿārif calls him the inveterate enemy and persecutor of the Prophet ﷺ, who would stand up and cry lie to his message whenever he invited people to faith.

Why does the Qur'an use the nickname and not the real name? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons: his actual name smacked of paganism; and the element *lahab*, "flame," in his nickname has a connection with the flame of Hell. The name he was known by becomes the sentence passed on him.

Ibn Kathir also preserves an eyewitness memory. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abū az-Zinād that Rabīʿah ibn ʿAbbād of Banū ad-Dīl — a man of the pre-Islamic period who later accepted Islam — said: "I saw the Prophet ﷺ in the time of pre-Islamic ignorance in the market of Dhul-Majāz and he was saying, *'O people! Say there is no god worthy of worship except Allah and you will be successful.'* The people were gathered around him and behind him there was a man with a bright face, squint eyes and two braids in his hair, saying, 'Verily, he is an apostate and a liar!' This man was following him around wherever he went." Rabīʿah asked who it was. They said: "This is his uncle, Abu Lahab." Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad was alone in recording this ḥadīth.

## Ayah 1: two sentences doing two different things

*Tabbat yadā Abī Lahabin wa tabb.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the verb **tabba** comes from *tabāb*, meaning "to perish." And the two halves of the ayah are not saying the same thing twice:

- **"Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab"** — this is a prayer, an imprecation of destruction against him.
- **"and perish he"** — this is a declarative sentence, prophesying the consequence of that invocation.

Ibn Kathir puts it identically: "The first part is a supplication against him and the second is information about him."

Maʿārif adds something tender about why the du'ā form was used at all: when Abu Lahab called down destruction on the Prophet ﷺ, it was the desire of the Muslims that destruction be invoked against him. Allah fulfilled their desire — and in the same breath informed them that the invocation had taken effect and he had perished.

**Why "hands"?** Maʿārif notes that *yad* literally means "hand," but because hands play such an important role in human work and action, the word often stands for the person himself — as in *"All this is due to what your hands have sent forth"* (22:10). There is also a pointed reason. Al-Bayhaqī recorded on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās that Abu Lahab once told people that Muḥammad says such-and-such will happen after death — then, pointing to his own hands, said that none of those things had ever come into them, and addressed them: *"Perish you! I do not see any of the things Muḥammad said in you."* He cursed his own hands for showing him no evidence of the unseen. Maʿārif concludes: therefore the Qur'an attributes his destruction to his hands.

**What actually happened to him.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Bayān-ul-Qurʼān from Rūḥ) records that seven days after the battle of Badr he developed a terrible case of plague. People regarded it as infectious, avoided all contact, and forced him to live in an isolated house. He died in that state. His body lay untouched in his house for three days until it began to rot and give out an unbearable stench; people taunted his sons, who hired labourers to take it away and bury it. They dug a pit, pushed the body in with a stick, and covered it with stones. The man who mocked a warning about the Hereafter was buried without a hand laid on him.

## Ayah 2: the two things he was counting on

*"Neither his wealth nor what he earned will benefit him."*

The phrase **mā kasab** — "what he earned" — carries two readings, and both are in the sources:

1. The profits that accrued to him from investing his wealth in business (Maʿārif).
2. **His children.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others: "*Kasab* means his children," and a similar statement is reported from ʿĀ'ishah, Mujāhid, ʿAṭā', al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grounds the second reading in the Arabic idiom and in a report from ʿĀ'ishah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The best and the purest thing a man eats is from his earnings, and his children are part of his earnings"* — cited there from Qurṭubī. So a man's children genuinely count as his *kasb*, his earning. Maʿārif names ʿĀ'ishah, Mujāhid, ʿAṭā' and Ibn Sīrīn among those who read *mā kasab* as "children."

And that reading has teeth, because of what Abu Lahab actually said. Ibn Kathir mentions it from Ibn Masʿūd (Maʿārif reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās): when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called his people to faith and warned them of the punishment, Abu Lahab said, **"Even if what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from the painful torment on the Day of Judgement with my wealth and my children."** Ayah 2 is the direct reply. Maʿārif notes that Allah had in fact granted him abundant wealth and many children — and that these two factors led him to be ungrateful, proud and arrogant. When the Divine torment seized him in this world, neither one benefited him.

## Ayah 3: the flame in his name

*"He will burn in a flaming Fire."*

Ibn Kathir explains *nāran dhāta lahab*: "it has flames, evil and severe burning." Maʿārif points out the rhetorical relationship the ayah is making — the man called **Abu Lahab** enters a fire **dhāta lahab**. The nickname he wore for the glow of his face becomes the description of what will consume him.

Maʿārif also notes a difference over timing: this may be either on the Day of Judgement, or immediately after his death while in the grave, that he is pushed into the blazing fire.

## Ayat 4–5: the wife who carried the wood

Ibn Kathir identifies her: she was among the leading women of Quraysh, known as **Umm Jamīl**, her name **ʿArwah bint Ḥarb ibn Umayyah**, the sister of Abū Sufyān. "She was supportive of her husband in his disbelief, rejection and obstinacy."

**"The carrier of firewood"** — *ḥammālat al-ḥaṭab* — is read in three complementary ways by the commentators:

- **Tale-bearer.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Arabs use this expression idiomatically for a tale-bearer: one who gathers pieces of gossip and carries them between individuals and families in order to ignite the fires of discord and enmity, exactly as one would gather firewood to kindle a fire. She carried information about the private affairs of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the blessed Companions in an attempt to instigate trouble. This is the reading of **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah** and a group of commentators (Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathir).
- **Literally.** **Ibn Zayd, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk** and other commentators retain the original sense: she used to collect thorny branches from the jungle and place them in the path of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in order to harm him. Ibn Kathir reports this from al-ʿAwfī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭiyyah al-Jadalī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn Zayd.
- **In the Hereafter.** Ibn Kathir: because she was supportive of her husband, she will be helping to administer his punishment in the fire of Hell on the Day of Judgement — carrying the firewood and throwing it upon him to increase the torment he is in, "ready and prepared to do so." Maʿārif (citing Ibn Kathir) adds that she will collect the branches of *zaqqūm* and other trees and add them as fuel to the fire in which her husband is roasting.

**The rope in ayah 5.** Maʿārif works through the word: read *masd* (with sukūn) it is an infinitive meaning to twist a rope or cord strongly and tightly; read *masad* it refers to fibres — a rope of twisted palm fibre, or tightly braided coconut fibre, or a cord strongly woven, or a coil or cable formed by winding iron strands together (al-Qāmūs). Ibn Kathir quotes al-Jawharī to the same effect: *al-Masad* refers to fibres, and to rope made from fibres or palm leaves, or from the skins of camels or their furs.

The scholars then differ on which sense is meant:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUrwah ibn az-Zubayr and others** (via Mazharī) take it as a rope formed by twisting iron strands: an iron collar around her neck in Hell. Mujāhid, in the same report, reads *min masad* as *min ḥadīd*, "of iron." Ibn Kathir quotes Mujāhid: "This means a collar of iron. Don't you see that the Arabs call a pulley cable a *masad*?" Ibn Kathir also cites Mujāhid and ʿUrwah as saying, "From the palm fibre of the Fire."
- **Shaʿbī, Muqātil** and other commentators take it as a rope of twisted palm fibre, and read the ayah as a portrait of her meanness: though she and her husband were extremely wealthy and looked upon as leaders of their nation, out of her mean disposition and miserliness she would collect firewood from the jungle, bind it, place the bundle on her head and put the rope round her neck so it would not fall — and this practice led to her destruction, when she sat down exhausted, fell, was choked and died.

Maʿārif notes that most commentators preferred the first interpretation, since such conduct in Abu Lahab's family was hardly conceivable — and closes, as the scholars do when the evidence does not settle it: **Allah knows best.**

Either way, the image is exact: a woman of high Qurayshī rank, who thought herself above the Prophet ﷺ, with a coarse rope around her neck.

## When she came looking for him ﷺ

Ibn Kathir records through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from Asmā' bint Abī Bakr: when *"Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab"* was revealed, the one-eyed Umm Jamīl bint Ḥarb came out wailing with a stone in her hand, saying, "He criticizes our father, and his religion is our scorn, and his command is to disobey us." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting in the Masjid of the Kaʿbah and Abū Bakr was with him. When Abū Bakr saw her he said, "O Messenger of Allah! She is coming and I fear that she will see you." He ﷺ replied: **"Verily, she will not see me."** Then he recited some of the Qur'an as a protection for himself, as Allah says: *"And when you recite the Qur'an, We put between you and those who believe not in the Hereafter, an invisible veil"* (17:45).

She advanced until she was standing in front of Abū Bakr — and did not see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. She said, "O Abū Bakr! I have been informed that your friend is making defamatory poetry about me." Abū Bakr replied, "Nay! By the Lord of this House, he is not defaming you." So she turned away saying, "Indeed the Quraysh know that I am the daughter of their leader."

She left still holding her lineage. That was all she had.

## Living it

**Take tale-bearing seriously.** This is the one practical warning the sources themselves draw out of the passage at length. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that it is recorded in the two Ṣaḥīḥs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that a tale-bearer will not enter Paradise. Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ said three evil deeds destroy all of a man's righteous actions: backbiting, tale-bearing, and lying. And ʿAṭā' ibn as-Sā'ib once cited to Shaʿbī the tradition that three will not enter Paradise — a murderer, a tale-bearer, and a trader involved in usury — and asked in astonishment how a tale-bearer could be listed alongside the other two. Shaʿbī answered: **"Indeed, tale-bearing is the root cause of murder and usurpation of wealth."** (Qurṭubī.) Words carried between people are not small. They are firewood.

**Wealth and children are not a shield.** Abu Lahab's plan was to ransom himself with his wealth and his children. Ayah 2 says, in four words, that the plan does not exist. What Allah gives can become the very thing that makes a person arrogant — Maʿārif says exactly that of Abu Lahab's abundant wealth and many children.

**Closeness of blood saves no one.** He was the Prophet's ﷺ uncle. He shared the noblest lineage in Makkah with him. It bought him nothing, because he set himself against the truth.

**And Allah protects His Messenger ﷺ.** Umm Jamīl came out with a stone in her hand, looking for him, and stood right in front of Abū Bakr without seeing him — the Prophet ﷺ had said she would not, and recited Qur'an as a protection. Abu Lahab called down ruin on him; Maʿārif tells us the Muslims longed for that same imprecation to be turned back, and Allah both invoked it and told them it had already taken effect. Abu Lahab's mockery was a moment. The answer to it is part of the Qur'an, recited ever since.
